title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall)

title: Orientation-Tunable Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Lateral MoSe2/MoS2 Heterostructures: A Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics Study
abstract: Managing heat flow across interfaces in lateral 2D transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures is a key challenge for next-generation nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. To tackle this, we trained a deep learning interatomic potential (DLP) using DeePMD-kit on density functional theory (DFT) data, then paired it with non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations to study interfacial thermal conductance (ITC) in lateral MoSe$_2$/MoS$_2$ heterostructures, considering both armchair and zigzag interface orientations. The potential we trained closely matches DFT energies, forces, and phonon dispersion relations, which confirms its reliability for thermal transport simulations. Examining cell lengths from 10 to 40 nm and extrapolating to infinite length, the armchair interface shows a higher ITC (473 MW/m$^2$K) than the zigzag interface (387 MW/m$^2$K), and the armchair interface remains higher at every length considered. Both increase further as temperature rises. At 300 K, the vibrational density of states shows greater phonon spectral overlap at the armchair interface than at the zigzag interface. Together, these results offer a solid machine-learning framework for studying heat transport in lateral TMD heterostructures, and identify interface orientation as an effective means of controlling heat dissipation at these junctions.
comments: 13 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter

title: Application of Pretrained Universal Machine Learning Force-Fields for Phase Transitions Prediction in ZrO2
abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning force fields can reduce the cost of finite-temperature molecular dynamics relative to density functional theory. However, most benchmarks test only static properties and do not assess whether these models reproduce the correct phase-transition sequence. Here, we benchmark ten open-source universal machine-learning force fields for zirconia (ZrO$_2$) using phonon dispersion calculations and variable-cell isothermal-isobaric molecular dynamics. Zirconia is a useful test because it has three thermodynamically stable crystalline phases prior to melting, following the sequence monoclinic-tetragonal-cubic. Four models reproduce this sequence: 7net-l3i5, MatterSim-v1.0.0-1M, MACE-mpa, and MACE-D3. Models with orthorhombic-tetragonal energy errors above about 10 meV/atom (7net-0, CHGNet, and MACE) instead produce an orthorhombic intermediate and predict monoclinic-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic-liquid upon heating. ORB-based models fail to sustain stable variable-cell dynamics because their phonon frequencies are compressed by 30-60% relative to the density functional theory reference. Across all ten models, two ground-state diagnostics predict finite-temperature behavior. Relative polymorph energetics should agree with the matched density functional theory reference within about 6 meV/atom, and the phonon spectrum should not show systematic softening. These diagnostics are practical screening metrics for assessing pretrained force fields for phase-transition predictions.
comments: 23 pages, 13 figures, 1 supplementary table, 7 supplementary figures. Supplementary Material included

title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Disordered Systems and Neural Networks (cond-mat.dis-nn); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
abstract: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC$^{(1)}$ in 1D
abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to $512$ qubits for Clifford circuits with $768$ $T$-gates and up to $22$ qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

title: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon
abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.

title: Degree and normalization frontiers for bounded QSVT inversion
abstract: Quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) implements matrix inversion using bounded polynomials. Increasing polynomial degree can improve normalization and reduce amplified query cost, with savings that depend on the error criterion. However, existing bounded methods either fix the normalization or work far below the condition numbers of fault-tolerant resource estimates. We therefore analyze this trade-off for absolute reciprocal error, which controls inverse-operator accuracy, and for residual error, which suffices for normalized linear solves. For absolute reciprocal error, we establish a scaling limit to a constrained least-norm problem for entire functions and characterize its high-accuracy frontier using elliptic integrals. Constructions built from near-optimal limiting functions achieve certified query-cost savings over the rescaled minimax baseline of at least 11.8 percent at condition number ten thousand with error one millionth, and at least 22.8 percent at one million with error one ten-billionth. A simpler two-term rule also has certified savings, and its phase factors at condition number ten thousand pass numerical checks at selected points. For residual error, a sparse Chebyshev construction achieves certified savings over the residual-minimax baseline of at least 8.7 percent at condition number ten thousand with normalized-state error at most one hundred-millionth, and at least 13.1 percent at one million with error at most one ten-billionth. These results quantify the saving that a joint choice of degree and normalization gives beyond the minimax baselines.
comments: 22 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. The Supplemental Material (82 pages) and a public verification set are ancillary files

title: High-rate low-distance color codes
abstract: Experimental implementations of two-dimensional color codes encoding a single logical qubit have surpassed the fidelity of physical qubits. A natural next step is to investigate higher-rate codes that encode multiple logical qubits. Here we propose small, high-rate 2D color codes for this purpose. We design distance-$3$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/3$ and distance-$4$ codes with encoding rates up to $1/4$. We prove that these rates are optimal for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with non-negative Euler characteristic. We benchmark the codes by simulating Steane-style error correction with real-time feedback and no post-selection in a linear trapped-ion chain model with all-to-all connectivity. The two best-performing codes have parameters $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ and achieve break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$, respectively. These results match the performance of Shor-style error correction with bivariate bicycle codes that use weight-$5$ measurements.

title: Stabilizer models of achiral abelian topological orders
abstract: We construct continuous-variable stabilizer codes realizing every achiral 2D abelian topological order, both bosonic and fermionic. Starting from an arbitrary signature-zero integer $K$-matrix, we show that the corresponding topological order can be obtained by condensing a lattice of dyons with trivial pairwise mutual braiding in an $\mathbb{R}^N$ gauge theory. We implement this condensation microscopically by gauging a non-on-site 1-form symmetry of the $\mathbb{R}^N$ toric code.
subjects: Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el) ; High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th); Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
abstract: Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.

title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
abstract: Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ logical qubits, where $\epsilon$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$.
comments: Reader's guide included at the end of section 1

title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
abstract: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $\Omega_\epsilon(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-\epsilon}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<\epsilon<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $\gamma \rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-\epsilon}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $\Omega_\epsilon(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Information Theory (cs.IT); Mathematical Physics (math-ph)

title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
abstract: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.
comments: Main text (8 pages, 6 figures), supplement (16 pages, 7 figures)

title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 10 authors
abstract: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.
comments: 25 pages, 8 figures (4 in the main text, 4 in the Supplementary Information)

title: Atomic-scale assembly of sulfur vacancy complexes for tailored in-gap states in monolayer WS$_{2}$
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 7 authors
abstract: Atomic-scale defects in two-dimensional semiconductors are quasi-isolated quantum systems with promise for emerging technologies. Although their potential as spin qubits, quantum sensors and single-photon emitters has been demonstrated experimentally, creating them deterministically and identifying them chemically remains challenging, which limits control over their electronic states. In this work we assemble sulfur vacancies in monolayer WS$_{2}$ into complexes of different sizes and geometries using the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. We study their electronic properties by a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory, revealing the intricate influences of geometry, underlying point group symmetries and spin-orbit coupling on hybridized states. Among the realized sulfur vacancy complexes, we characterize two configurations that are candidates for bright single photon emitters. Our findings demonstrate an atomic-scale method for engineering quantum states within the band gap of two-dimensional semiconductors.

title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
abstract: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.

title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
abstract: How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $\epsilon$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.

title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms
abstract: The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.

title: Instanton tunnelling as a verifiable benchmark for digital quantum simulation: circuit structure, classical simulability and hardware reproducibility
abstract: We use instanton-mediated tunnelling in the quartic double well as a benchmark for digital quantum simulation that is checkable against an exact answer at every step. The instanton enters through the classical analysis; the hardware tests the dynamics of the lattice model. A unary (single-excitation) encoding maps N lattice sites to N qubits, with the single-excitation dynamics as a reference that remains classically cheap at any N. For a second-order Trotter circuit with adjacent, equal-angle XX/YY pairs on each bond, we prove that the Schmidt rank across any cut is at most four at every gate boundary and at most two after each pair, independently of N. Matrix-product-state simulations of this gate list reproduce the exact splitting up to N = 48. For this bond-wise formula the admissible Trotter step shrinks roughly as N^-2, so one tunnelling period costs about N^3.3 two-qubit gates; a kinetic/potential splitting keeps the step near 0.065 up to N=128, so this scaling belongs to splitting the kinetic term bond by bond. At a coarser, separately bounded step we measure the full transfer at N=8 on two superconducting processors, recovering the lattice splitting to a few percent and its dependence on the barrier height, which at this resolution is set by the lattice rather than by the instanton. Over 9 repetitions, runs taken minutes apart agree to shot noise, while runs hours to weeks apart differ by up to 6.1%, also on a fixed set of qubits; with sessions as the sampling unit, the processors differ in the damping, while a difference in the splitting is not established. Normalising by the measured single-excitation population extends the usable depth about 4-fold but does not improve the splitting. A Gaussian start state, which needs no diagonalisation, reproduces the splitting of the eigenvector-based start to within 1.6 percentage points.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; High Energy Physics - Phenomenology (hep-ph); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 9 authors
abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

title: On a local hidden-variable model for postselected EPR correlations
abstract: A theoretical and numerical analysis of a Bell-type experiment is presented, where linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled through a sigmoid-based threshold mechanism that violates the fair-sampling assumption required by the CHSH inequality. Numerical simulations characterize how closely this local construction can reproduce quantum-like correlations in the postselected detected sample, for both the |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states over a range of entanglement parameters. For the tested configurations, the model produces CHSH-type violations only in the postselected detected sample through a setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside the assumptions of both the CHSH inequality and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. The model is not in conflict with loophole-free Bell experiments, which specifically close the detection loophole exploited here. The CH--Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration yields J < 0 throughout the full range of entanglement parameters, as required for a strictly local model. The model is further extended with a local adaptive-threshold mechanism implementing one-sided memory. A paired comparison shows that this specific memory rule produces a systematic and reproducible shift in the CH--Eberhard parameter J relative to the fixed-threshold model, while leaving the CH--Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged under the tested conditions. The results characterize how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics across a range of entanglement parameters, within the specific configurations and threshold rules tested.

title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
abstract: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

title: Qubit-qumode simulation of molecular torsion in photoisomerization
abstract: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations, so the framework extends naturally to larger systems.

title: Bound entanglement as a trigonometric moment problem
abstract: Entangled states that are positive under partial transposition (PPT) are the main obstruction to a simple description of entanglement. We study three basic questions about them within a class of multiqubit states, the mixtures, with real but possibly negative weights, of products of equatorial spin coherent states of several groups of qubits: which PPT entangled states belong to the class, how robust their entanglement is to white noise, and how small their rank can be. In this class each question becomes a question about a truncated trigonometric moment problem. Every such state is PPT across every bipartition, and it is fully separable exactly when an associated multi-level Toeplitz matrix is the moment matrix of a positive measure on the torus. We answer the three questions exactly in the following cases. For three qubits, every rank-four PPT entangled state with nonzero Lorentz invariant belongs to the class after invertible local operators, which proves a working hypothesis of Garberg, Irgens and Myrheim and yields a complete set of invariants for this seven-dimensional family; among the states with vanishing invariant, exactly a one-parameter family belongs to it. For every three-qubit state built from an unextendible product basis, the white-noise threshold for full separability is $\lambda^*=1-2/(1+\sqrt{1+s})$ with a local-unitary invariant $s\in(0,1]$, and $\lambda^*=3-2\sqrt2$ for the Shifts basis; a witness in closed form detects every entangled state of this family with eight local Pauli settings. For two groups of qubits we construct extremal states of minimal rank, and for three groups we determine the minimal rank of entanglement within the class in several configurations.

title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
abstract: Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $\kappa$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2\kappa$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $\chi^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $\kappa$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.

title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 8 authors
abstract: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
abstract: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.

title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 9 authors
abstract: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit $Z$ rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.
comments: 22 pages, 12 figures (4 main-text figures and 8 Extended Data figures), and 1 Extended Data table

title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
abstract: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.
comments: This is the pre-print version of the article to appear in SN Computer Science. Code will be released once manuscript is published

title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
abstract: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.

title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
abstract: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
abstract: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.
comments: Keywords: Qubit, forsterite, quantum gates, Fe$^{2+}$, zero-field splitting (ZFS), two-level system

title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Signal Processing (eess.SP)

title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
abstract: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|\psi\rangle$ with overlap at least $\gamma>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $\delta$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $\Delta$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ or $\Delta$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Omega(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ for GSEE and $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ for GSP, showing that $\sqrt{s}$ is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
abstract: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.
comments: This is the accepted, prepublication version of a paper forthcoming in Computer Music Journal, MIT Press. Beyond routine editorial and typesetting amendments, the content remains subject to further revision before final publication

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Education for Software Developers: A Multivocal Literature Review
abstract: Quantum computing threatens widely deployed public-key cryptography, making post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adoption a software engineering challenge. However, it remains unclear how well existing educational provision prepares software developers for secure PQC implementation and migration. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 8 research publications and 15 professional training offerings, examining competency coverage, practical software engineering tasks, pedagogical approaches, learner support, and evaluation. All 23 sources covered PQC foundations and algorithms, but coverage of practical software-engineering tasks was uneven. Our analysis identifies six gaps concerning developer focused evaluation, authentic software engineering tasks, task competency alignment, pedagogical design and learner support, security-focused assessment, and long term validation of learning outcomes and transfer. We derive recommendations for strengthening PQC education and better preparing software developers to implement and migrate cryptographic systems securely.

title: A Convex-Roof Affinity-Square Measure of Quantum Imaginarity
abstract: Quantum imaginarity characterizes the part of a quantum state that cannot be represented by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. We study an affinity-square measure of imaginarity for pure states and its convex-roof extension to mixed states. The pure state quantity is defined by minimizing the affinity-square measure over the convex set of real states. This optimization admits a closed expression determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between a state and its complex conjugate. The measure vanishes precisely when the state is real up to a global phase. We prove that the convex-roof extension is faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states, we evaluate the convex roof exactly and express it in terms of the imaginary component of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. We also compare pure-state imaginarity with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional and give the corresponding phase weights.

title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
abstract: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(\rho(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_\rho(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_\rho(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_\rho(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces for Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
abstract: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and $g_{\rm sm}/(2\pi)=3.81\,\mathrm{kHz}$, a mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.

title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 8 authors
abstract: We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.

title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.
comments: 27 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Main text with Methods, followed by Supplementary Information

title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
abstract: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(\lambda^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $\lambda$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(\lambda^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.

title: Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons
abstract: Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.

title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
abstract: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{\Omega(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. ( arXiv:2504.14841 ), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
abstract: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95.
